title: Japji 1–7, whole
hookLine: the wall of falsehood, the order, the Giver, the early hours
tomorrow: four pauris in a row start with the same word. which one?

lines: ONE EMAIL, READ AGAIN AND AGAIN.
SO WHAT DOES GET YOU THERE?
cards: An email lands, and you read it once. Then again. Then a third time, hunting for the tone.
By evening there are four drafted replies and none sent. Guru Nanak names this exact loop in the Japji's first pauri: sochai soch na hovaee je sochee lakh vaar.
Think it over a hundred thousand times, and thinking still won't get you there. So what does?

teach.b: Read pauris one to seven in one sitting, and a single thread holds them: hukam, the order, the Will running through everything. Pauri one asks the question straight out: kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai, kiv koorrai tuttai paal.

teach.h: HOW DOES THE WALL COME DOWN?
teach.b: How does the wall of falsehood come down? Its last line answers: hukam rajaaee chalanaa. Walk in the order, the Will.
Pauri two: everything is inside the order, nothing outside it.
Pauri three: people sing of the Giver in endless ways, and the Giver keeps giving while the takers grow tired. Pauri four: the true Lord, and the early hours for the true Name.
Pauri five: the One can't be installed or made, and the plea, may I not forget the one Giver of all. Pauri six: bathing at pilgrim places counts only if it pleases the One.
Pauri seven: even a life four ages long, known in every land, means nothing without grace. Read whole, it works like a loosening.
Overthinking, cleverness, ritual, fame: each one gets set down in turn.
What's left isn't a technique. It's a direction.

how: Sikhs who keep nitnem recite the whole Japji in the morning as the first of the daily banis, from a gutka or from memory, reading straight through from pauri to pauri.

o: the first seven letters of the Gurmukhi alphabet
the seven rules a new Sikh learns at amrit
the Japji's first seven pauris, read in one sitting

games.q: pauris one to seven — tap the pairs.
p: walk in the order, the Will
the Giver gives; the takers tire
may I not forget the one Giver
a long, well-known life means nothing alone

s: the Japji's first pauri praises hard thinking as the path to truth
thinking a lakh times won't get you there, it says; walk in the order.
pauri five asks not to forget the one Giver of all
the one Giver of all beings: may I not forget.
pauri seven says a long and well-known life is enough on its own
even a life four ages long, known in every land, means nothing without grace.

games.q: a friend tries a day of total silence to feel closer to God, and feels nothing. what does pauri one say about that?
o: silence alone, like thinking alone, won't do it; pauri one points to walking in the Will.
she should keep it up longer; pauri one says effort builds until it works.
the Japji forbids silent practice, so she should drop it entirely.
games.why: pauri one names thinking, silence, appetite and cleverness, and says none alone gets you there. its answer is hukam rajaaee chalanaa: walk in the order.

practice: Open the Japji, in a gutka, an app or on a printed page, and read from pauri one onward at an easy pace, in Gurmukhi or English. Don't stop to study a line.
When the sit ends, stop where you are, and let the last line you read be the one you keep.

carryVoice: Something to keep: walk in the order, which no amount of thinking can replace. Two of the summit.
